question: Billy is hiking in Colorado. He walks eastward four miles, then turns 60 degrees northward and walks six miles. How far is he from his starting point? Express your answer in simplest radical form.
solution: Suppose Billy starts at point A, turns at point B, and ends at point D, as shown below. If Billy turns 60^∘ northward and walks six miles, then we can draw a 30-60-90 triangle whose hypotenuse is 6 miles (triangle BCD below). [asy] size(150); defaultpen(linewidth(0.7) + fontsize(10)); pair A,B,C,D; A = (0,0); B=(4,0); C =(7,0); D = (7,3*sqrt(3)); draw (A–B–D–A); draw(B–C–D,dashed); label("A",A,S); label("B",B,S); label("4",B/2,S); label("6",(B+D)/2,NW); label("C",C,S); label("D",D,N); [/asy] It follows that Billy traveled 6/2 = 3 miles eastward during these 6 miles, and that he traveled 3 ·√(3) miles northward during these 6 miles. In total, Billy traveled 4 + 3 = 7 miles eastward and 3√(3) miles northward. By the Pythagorean Theorem, the distance from his starting point is √((7)^2 + (3√(3))^2) = √(49 + 27) = √(76) = 2√(19).

question: A 6 cm by 8 cm rectangle is inscribed in a circle. What is the number of centimeters in the circumference of the circle? Express your answer in terms of π. [asy]import graph; defaultpen(linewidth(0.7)); draw(Circle((0,0),20)); draw((-16,-12)–(16,-12)–(16,12)–(-16,12)–cycle); [/asy]
solution: Draw a diagonal of the rectangle. By the Pythagorean theorem, the length of the diagonal is √(6^2+8^2)=10 centimeters. Also, by symmetry the diagonal of the rectangle is a diameter of the circle. The circumference of the circle is π× (diameter)=10π centimeters. [asy] import graph; defaultpen(linewidth(0.7)); draw(Circle((0,0),20)); draw((-16,-12)–(16,-12)–(16,12)–(-16,12)–cycle); draw((16,-12)–(-16,12)); draw(rightanglemark((16,-12),(16,12),(-16,12),45));[/asy]

question: In the figure, ∠ ABC and ∠ ADB are each right angles. Additionally, AC = 17.8 units and AD = 5 units. What is the length of segment DB? [asy] import olympiad; import geometry; size(150); defaultpen(linewidth(0.8)); triangle t = triangle((0,0),(sqrt(89),0),(sqrt(89),-8/5*sqrt(89))); draw((sqrt(89),0)–(5*dir(-aTan(8/5)))); draw(t); dot("A",(0,0),W); dot("B",(sqrt(89),0),E); dot("D",5*dir(-aTan(8/5)),W); dot("C",17.8*dir(-aTan(8/5)),W); [/asy]
solution: First of all, we calculate that the length of DC is 17.8 - 5 = 12.8. Since triangles ADB and BDC are similar, BD/AD is equal to CD/BD, giving us the equation x/5 = 12.8/x. Multiplying both sides by 5x, we get x^2 = 64, so x = 8 units.

question: A triangle is made of wood sticks of lengths 8, 15 and 17 inches joined end-to-end. Pieces of the same integral length are cut from each of the sticks so that the three remaining pieces can no longer form a triangle. How many inches are in the length of the smallest piece that can be cut from each of the three sticks to make this happen?
solution: Our current triangle lengths are 8, 15, and 17. Let us say that x is the length of the piece that we cut from each of the three sticks. Then, our lengths will be 8 - x, 15 - x, and 17 - x. These lengths will no longer form a triangle when the two shorter lengths added together is shorter than or equal to the longest length. In other words, (8 - x) + (15 - x) ≤ (17 - x). Then, we have 23 - 2x ≤ 17 - x, so 6 ≤ x. Therefore, the length of the smallest piece that can be cut from each of the three sticks is 6 inches.

question: In ABC points D and E lie on BC and AC, respectively. If AD and BE intersect at T so that AT/DT=3 and BT/ET=4, what is CD/BD? [asy] pair A,B,C,D,I,T; A=(0,0); B=(6,8); C=(11,0); D=(9.33,2.66); I=(7.5,0); T=(6.5,2); label("T",T,NW); label("D",D,NE); label("E",I,S); label("A",A,S); label("C",C,S); label("B",B,N); draw(A–B–C–cycle,linewidth(0.7)); draw(A–D,linewidth(0.7)); draw(B–I,linewidth(0.7)); [/asy]
solution: Let F be a point on AC such that DF is parallel to BE. Let BT = 4x and ET=x. [asy] pair A,B,C,D,I,T,F; A=(0,0); B=(6,8); C=(11,0); D=(9.33,2.66); I=(7.5,0); T=(6.5,2); F=(9.9,0); draw(D–F,linewidth(0.7)); label("4x",(6.5,5.67),W); label("x",(7.35,0.8),W); label("F",F,S); label("T",T,NW); label("D",D,NE); label("E",I,S); label("A",A,S); label("C",C,S); label("B",B,N); draw(A–B–C–cycle,linewidth(0.7)); draw(A–D,linewidth(0.7)); draw(B–I,linewidth(0.7)); [/asy] Because ATE and ADF are similar, we have DF/x = AD/AT = 4/3, and DF=4x/3. Also, BEC and DFC are similar, so CD/BC =DF/BE = 4x/3/5x = 4/15. Thus CD/BD = CD/BC/1-(CD/BC)= 4/15/1- 4/15= 4/11.

question: In the figure below, a 3-inch by 3-inch square adjoins a 10-inch by 10-inch square. What is the area of the shaded region? Express your answer in square inches as a common fraction. [asy] unitsize(2mm); defaultpen(linewidth(0.7pt)+fontsize(12pt)); pair H=(0,0), A=(0,10), B=(10,10), C=(10,3), G=(10,0), E=(13,3), F=(13,0); pair D=extension(A,F,B,G); draw(A–B–G–H–cycle); fill(D–C–E–F–cycle, black); draw(A–F); draw(G–F–E–C); label("A",A,NW); label("H",H,SW); label("B",B,NE); label("C",C,NE); label("G",G,S); label("D",D,WSW); label("E",E,NE); label("F",F,SE); [/asy]
solution: Since triangle DGF is similar to triangle AHF, we have DG/GF=AH/HF. Substituting we find DG/3=10/10+3, which we solve to get DG=30/13 inches. The area of triangle DGF is 1/2(30/13)(3)=45/13 square inches. The area of the 3 in.×3 in. square is 9 square inches, so the area of the shaded region is 9-45/13=72/13 square inches.

question: In the triangle shown, what is the positive difference between the greatest and least possible integral values of x? [asy] defaultpen(linewidth(0.7)); pair a,b,c; b = (1,2); c = (3,0); draw(a–b–c–a); label("x",a–b,dir(135)); label("5",b–c,dir(45)); label("6",c–a,S); [/asy]
solution: We have x<6+5=11 and x>6-5=1, so the possible values of x are from 2 to 10, and their difference is 10-2 = 8.

question: Joe has exactly enough paint to paint the surface of a cube whose side length is 2. It turns out that this is also exactly enough paint to paint the surface of a sphere. If the volume of this sphere is K √(6)/√(π), then what is K?
solution: Since the cube has six sides, each of area 2^2 = 4, the surface area of the cube is 24. Since Joe's paint will exactly cover the cube and it will also exactly cover the sphere, the sphere also must have surface area 24. If r is the radius of the sphere, this tells us that 4 π r^2 = 24 , or r^2 = 6/π, so r = √(6/π) = √(6)/√(π). Therefore the volume of the sphere is 4/3π r^3 =4/3π( √(6)/√(π))^3 = 4/3π·6 √(6)/π√(π) = 8 √(6)/√(π) . Thus K=8.

question: The sides of triangle CAB are in the ratio of 2:3:4. Segment BD is the angle bisector drawn to the shortest side, dividing it into segments AD and DC. What is the length, in inches, of the longer subsegment of side AC if the length of side AC is 10 inches? Express your answer as a common fraction.
solution: Without loss of generality, suppose that BA < BC. Since BD is the angle bisector of ∠ B, by the Angle Bisector Theorem, it follows that AD/CD = BA/BC = 3/4. Thus, AD < CD, so CD is the longer subsegment of AC. Solving for AD, it follows that AD = 3CD/4. Also, we know that AD + CD = AC = 10, and substituting our previous value for AD, we find that 3CD/4 + CD = 7CD/4 = 10 ⟹ CD = 40/7 inches.

question: What is the radius of the circle inscribed in triangle ABC if AB = 5, AC=6, BC=7? Express your answer in simplest radical form.
solution: Let r be the radius of the inscribed circle. Let s be the semiperimeter of the triangle, that is, s=AB+AC+BC/2=9. Let K denote the area of ABC. Heron's formula tells us that K = √(s(s-AB)(s-AC)(s-BC)) = √(9· 4· 3· 2) = √(3^3· 2^3) = 6√(6). The area of a triangle is equal to its semiperimeter multiplied by the radius of its inscribed circle (K=rs), so we have 6√(6) = r· 9, which yields the radius r=2√(6)/3.

question: Find the number of cubic centimeters in the volume of the cylinder formed by rotating a square with side length 14 centimeters about its vertical line of symmetry. Express your answer in terms of π.
solution: [asy] size(100); draw((-5,-.2)–(-3,-.2)–(-3,1.8)–(-5,1.8)–cycle); label("14",((-3,1.8)–(-5,1.8)),N); label("14",((-5,-.2)–(-5,1.8)),W); draw((-2.5,.9)–(-1.5,.9),EndArrow); import solids; import three; currentprojection = orthographic(5,0,2); revolution c = cylinder((0,0,0), 1, 2); draw((0,-1,2)–(0,1,2)); label("14",((0,-1,2)–(0,1,2)),N); label("14",(0,1,1),E); draw(c,black); [/asy] Rotating the square about its vertical line of symmetry creates a right circular cylinder with diameter 14 and height 14. Thus, the cylinder has radius 14/2=7 and volume π(7^2)(14)=π(50-1)(14)=π(700-14)=686π.

question: If an arc of 45^∘ on circle A has the same length as an arc of 30^∘ on circle B, then what is the ratio of the area of circle A to the area of circle B? Express your answer as a common fraction.
solution: Let C_A= 2π R_A be the circumference of circle A, let C_B= 2π R_B be the circumference of circle B, and let L the common length of the two arcs. Then 45/360C_A = L = 30/360C_B. Therefore C_A/C_B = 2/3 so 2/3=2π R_A/2π R_B =R_A/R_B. Thus, the ratio of the areas is Area of Circle (A)/Area of Circle (B) =π R_A^2/π R_B^2 = (R_A/R_B)^2 =4/9.

question: In the adjoining figure, CD is the diameter of a semicircle with center O. Point A lies on the extension of DC past C; point E lies on the semicircle, and B is the point of intersection (distinct from E) of line segment AE with the semicircle. If length AB equals length OD, and the measure of ∠ EOD is 45^∘, then find the measure of ∠ BAO, in degrees. [asy] import graph; unitsize(2 cm); pair O, A, B, C, D, E; O = (0,0); C = (-1,0); D = (1,0); E = dir(45); B = dir(165); A = extension(B,E,C,D); draw(arc(O,1,0,180)); draw(D–A–E–O); label("A", A, W); label("B", B, NW); label("C", C, S); label("D", D, S); label("E", E, NE); label("O", O, S); [/asy]
solution: Draw BO. Let y = ∠ BAO. Since AB = OD = BO, triangle ABO is isosceles, so ∠ BOA = ∠ BAO = y. Angle ∠ EBO is exterior to triangle ABO, so ∠ EBO = ∠ BAO + ∠ BOA = y + y = 2y. [asy] import graph; unitsize(2 cm); pair O, A, B, C, D, E; O = (0,0); C = (-1,0); D = (1,0); E = dir(45); B = dir(165); A = extension(B,E,C,D); draw(arc(O,1,0,180)); draw(D–A–E–O); draw(B–O); label("A", A, W); label("B", B, NW); label("C", C, S); label("D", D, S); label("E", E, NE); label("O", O, S); [/asy] Triangle BEO is isosceles, so ∠ BEO = ∠ EBO = 2y. Then ∠ EOD is external to triangle AEO, so ∠ EOD = ∠ EAO + ∠ AEO = y + 2y = 3y. But ∠ EOD = 45^∘, so ∠ BAO = y = 45^∘/3 = 15^∘.

question: When each edge of a cube is increased by 50%, by what percent is the surface area of the cube increased?
solution: Let s represent the length of the edge of a cube. The surface area of the cube is 6 times the area of each face (since there are 6 faces), or 6s^2. Increasing s by 50% gives us 1.5s. The new surface area is 6(1.5s)^2=6s^2(2.25). Increasing the surface area by x% is 6s^2(1+x/100), so we solve for x when the surface area is 6s^2(2.25). 2.25=1+x/100 ⇒ 1.25=x/100 ⇒ 125=x The surface area increases by 125%.

question: A solid right prism ABCDEF has a height of 16, as shown. Also, its bases are equilateral triangles with side length 12. Points X, Y, and Z are the midpoints of edges AC, BC, and DC, respectively. A part of the prism above is sliced off with a straight cut through points X, Y, and Z. Determine the surface area of solid CXYZ, the part that was sliced off. [asy] pair A, B, C, D, E, F, X, Y, Z; A=(0,0); B=(12,0); C=(6,-6); D=(6,-22); E=(0,-16); F=(12,-16); X=(A+C)/2; Y=(B+C)/2; Z=(C+D)/2; draw(A–B–C–A–E–D–F–B–C–D); draw(X–Y–Z–X, dashed); label("A", A, NW); label("B", B, NE); label("C", C, N); label("D", D, S); label("E", E, SW); label("F", F, SE); label("X", X, SW); label("Y", Y, SE); label("Z", Z, SE); label("12", (A+B)/2, dir(90)); label("16", (B+F)/2, dir(0)); [/asy]
solution: To determine the surface area of solid CXYZ, we determine the area of each of the four triangular faces and sum them. Areas of CZX and CZY: Each of these triangles is right-angled and has legs of lengths 6 and 8; therefore, the area of each is 1/2(6)(8)=24. Area of CXY: This triangle is equilateral with side length 6. We draw the altitude from C to M on XY. Since CXY is equilateral, then M is the midpoint of XY. Thus, CMX and CMY are 30^∘-60^∘-90^∘ triangles. Using the ratios from this special triangle, CM = √(3)/2(CX)=√(3)/2(6)=3√(3). Since XY = 6, the area of CXY is 1/2(6)(3√(3))=9√(3). Area of XYZ: We have XY = 6 and XZ = YZ = 10 and drop an altitude from Z to XY. Since XYZ is isosceles, this altitude meets XY at its midpoint, M, and we have XM = MY = 1/2(XY)=3. By the Pythagorean Theorem, ZM = √(ZX^2 - XM^2) = √(10^2-3^2) = √(91). Since XY = 6, the area of XYZ is 1/2(6)(√(91))=3√(91). Finally, the total surface area of solid CXYZ is 24+24+9√(3)+3√(91)=48+9√(3)+3√(91).

question: Let n equal the number of sides in a regular polygon. For 3≤ n < 10, how many values of n result in a regular polygon where the common degree measure of the interior angles is not an integer?
solution: The number of degrees is the sum of the interior angles of an n-gon is 180(n-2). If the n-gon is regular, then each angle measures 180(n-2)/n degrees. If n=3, 4, 5, 6, or 9, then n divides evenly into 180, so the number of degrees in each angle is an integer. If n=7, then the number of degrees is 180·5/7=900/7, which is not an integer. If n=8, the number of degrees in each angle is 180· 6/8=135. Therefore, only 1 value of n between 3 and 9 results in a non-integer degree measure for each interior angle of a regular n-gon.

question: Medians are drawn from point A and point B in this right triangle to divide segments BC and AC in half, respectively. The lengths of the medians are 6 and 2√(11) units, respectively. How many units are in the length of segment AB? [asy] draw((0,0)–(7,0)–(0,4)–(0,0)–cycle,linewidth(2)); draw((0,1/2)–(1/2,1/2)–(1/2,0),linewidth(1)); label("A",(0,4),NW); label("B",(7,0),E); label("C",(0,0),SW); [/asy]
solution: We draw the medians as shown below. [asy] draw((0,0)–(7,0)–(0,4)–(0,0)–cycle,linewidth(2)); draw((0,1/2)–(1/2,1/2)–(1/2,0),linewidth(1)); draw((0,4)–(3.5,0)); draw((0,2)–(7,0)); label("A",(0,4),NW); label("B",(7,0),E); label("C",(0,0),SW); label("M",(3.5,0),S); label("N",(0,2),W); [/asy] From right triangles ACM and BCN, we have AC^2 + CM^2 = 36, BC^2 + CN^2 = (2√(11))^2 = 44. However, we have CM = BC/2 and CN = AC/2, so the equations above become AC^2 + 1/4BC^2 = 36, BC^2 + 1/4AC^2 =44. Adding these equations gives 5/4(AC^2 + BC^2) = 80, so AC^2 + BC^2 = 64. But the Pythagorean Theorem gives us AB^2 = AC^2 + BC^2, so AB^2 = 64, which means AB = 8.

question: The diameter, in inches, of a sphere with twice the volume of a sphere of radius 9 inches can be expressed in the form a√(b) where a and b are positive integers and b contains no perfect cube factors. Compute a+b.
solution: A sphere with radius 9 inches has volume 4/3π(9^3)=4· 9^2 · 3π cubic inches; twice this is 8· 9^2· 3 π cubic inches. Let the radius of the larger sphere be r, so we have 4/3π r^3= 8· 9^2· 3π . Solving for r yields r^3 =2· 9^3 ⇒ r = 9√(2). The diameter is twice this value, or 18√(2) inches. Hence a=18, b=2, and a+b=20.

question: Triangles ABC and ADC are isosceles with AB=BC and AD=DC. Point D is inside ABC, ∠ ABC = 40^∘, and ∠ ADC = 140^∘. What is the degree measure of ∠ BAD?
solution: Because ABC is isosceles, ∠ BAC=1/2( 180^∘-∠ ABC)=70^∘. [asy] pair A,B,C,D; A=(-5,0); B=(0,21); C=(5,0); D=(0,6); draw(A–B–C–cycle,linewidth(1)); draw(A–D–C–cycle,linewidth(1)); label("140^∘",(0,4),S); label("40^∘",(0,15),S); label("A",A,W); label("B",B,N); label("C",C,E); label("D",D,N); [/asy] Similarly, ∠ DAC=1/2( 180^∘-∠ ADC)=20^∘. Thus ∠ BAD = ∠ BAC - ∠ DAC = 50^∘.

question: A solid box is 15 cm by 10 cm by 8 cm. A new solid is formed by removing a cube 3 cm on a side from each corner of this box. What percent of the original volume is removed?
solution: The total volume of the eight removed cubes is 8× 3^3=216 cubic centimeters, and the volume of the original box is 15× 10× 8 = 1200 cubic centimeters. Therefore the volume has been reduced by (216/1200)(100%) = 18%.

question: Regular hexagon ABCDEF has vertices A and C at (0,0) and (7,1), respectively. What is its area?
solution: Diagonals AC, CE, EA, AD, CF, and EB divide the hexagon into twelve congruent 30-60-90 triangles, six of which make up equilateral ACE. [asy] unitsize(0.5 cm); pair A, B, C, D, E, F, G; A = (0,0); C = (7,1); E = rotate(60)*(C); G = (A + C + E)/3; B = 2*G - E; D = 2*G - A; F = 2*G - C; draw(A–B–C–D–E–F–cycle); draw((-2,0)–(9,0)); draw((0,-2)–(0,8)); draw(A–C–E–cycle); draw(A–D); draw(B–E); draw(C–F); label("A", A, SW); label("B", B, S); label("C", C, dir(0)); label("D", D, NE); label("E", E, N); label("F", F, W); [/asy] Because AC=√(7^2+1^2)=√(50), the area of ACE is √(3)/4(√(50))^2=25/2√(3). The area of hexagon ABCDEF is 2(25/2√(3))=25√(3). An alternate way to start: let O be the center of the hexagon. Then triangles ABC,CDE, and EFA are congruent to triangles AOC,COE, and EOA, respectively. Thus the area of the hexagon is twice the area of equilateral ACE. Then proceed as in the first solution.

question: Five points A, B, C, D, and O lie on a flat field. A is directly north of O, B is directly west of O, C is directly south of O, and D is directly east of O. The distance between C and D is 140 m. A hot-air balloon is positioned in the air at H directly above O. The balloon is held in place by four ropes HA, HB, HC, and HD. Rope HC has length 150 m and rope HD has length 130 m. How high is the balloon above the field (that is, the length of OH)? [asy] size(200); pair A, B, C, D, O, H, W, X, Y, Z; O=(0,0); A=(1,1); D=(1.5,-.3); B=(-1.5,.3); C=(-1,-1); H=(0,2.5); W=(5/3)*(A+D); X=(5/3)*(A+B); Y=(-1)*(W); Z=(-1)*(X); draw(W–X–Y–Z–W); draw(A–C); draw(B–D); draw(O–H, linewidth(1)); draw(A–H, dashed); draw(B–H, dashed); draw(C–H, dashed); draw(D–H, dashed); dot(A); dot(B); dot(C); dot(D); dot(O); dot(H); label("A", A, NE); label("B", B, SW); label("C", C, SE); label("D", D, NE); label("O", O, SE); label("H", H, NW); [/asy]
solution: Let OC=c, OD=d and OH=h. [asy] size(200); pair A, B, C, D, O, H, W, X, Y, Z; O=(0,0); A=(1,1); D=(1.5,-.3); B=(-1.5,.3); C=(-1,-1); H=(0,2.5); W=(5/3)*(A+D); X=(5/3)*(A+B); Y=(-1)*(W); Z=(-1)*(X); draw(W–X–Y–Z–W); draw(A–C); draw(B–D); draw(O–H, linewidth(1)); draw(C–D, dashed); draw(C–H, dashed); draw(D–H, dashed); dot(C); dot(D); dot(O); dot(H); label("C", C, SE); label("D", D, NE); label("O", O, SE); label("H", H, NW); label("c", (C+O)/2, N); label("d", (D+O)/2, N); label("h", (O+H)/2, E); label("130", (H+D)/2, NE); label("140", (C+D)/2, S); label("150", (C+H)/2, NW); [/asy] Note that OH is perpendicular to the field, so OH is perpendicular to OC and to OD. Also, since OD points east and OC points south, then OD is perpendicular to OC. Since HC=150, we have h^2+c^2=150^2 by the Pythagorean Theorem. Since HD=130, we have h^2+d^2=130^2. Since CD=140, we have c^2+d^2 = 140^2. . Adding the first two equations, we obtain 2h^2+c^2+d^2=150^2+130^2. Since c^2+d^2=140^2, we have 2h^2 + 140^2 = 150^2+130^2 2h^2 = 150^2 + 130^2 - 140^2 2h^2 = 19800 h^2 = 9900 h = √(9900)=30√(11) Therefore, the height of the balloon above the field is 30√(11) meters.

question: For the quadrilateral shown, how many different whole numbers could be the length of the diagonal represented by the dashed line? [asy] draw((0,0)–(5,5)–(12,1)–(7,-8)–cycle,linewidth(0.7)); draw((0,0)–(12,1),dashed); label("8",(2.5,2.5),NW); label("10",(8.5,3),NE); label("16",(9.5, -3.5),SE); label("12",(3.5,-4),SW); [/asy]
solution: Label the vertices A, B, C, and D as shown, and let x = AC. [asy] draw((0,0)–(5,5)–(12,1)–(7,-8)–cycle,linewidth(0.7)); draw((0,0)–(12,1),dashed); label("8",(2.5,2.5),NW); label("10",(8.5,3),NE); label("16",(9.5, -3.5),SE); label("12",(3.5,-4),SW); label("A",(0,0),W); label("B",(5,5),N); label("C",(12,1),E); label("D",(7,-8),S); label("x", ((0,0) + (12,1))/2, N); [/asy] By the triangle inequality on triangle ABC, x + 8 > 10, x + 10 > 8, 8 + 10 > x, which tell us that x > 2, x > -2, and x < 18. By the triangle inequality on triangle CDA, x + 12 > 16, x + 16 > 12, 12 + 16 > x, which tell us that x > 4, x > -4, and x < 28. Therefore, the possible values of x are 5, 6, …, 17, for a total of 17 - 5 + 1 = 13.

question: In the figure below, if the area of ABC is 27, what is the value of p? [asy] size(5cm);defaultpen(fontsize(9)); pair o = (0, 0); pair q = (0, 12); pair b = (12, 0); pair a = (2, 12); pair t = (2, 0); pair c = (0, 9); draw((-2, 0)–(15, 0), Arrow); draw((0, -2)–(0, 15), Arrow); draw(q–a–b); //draw(a–t); draw(a–c–b); label("Q(0, 12)", q, W); label("A(2, 12)", a, NE); label("B(12, 0)", b, S); label("O(0, 0)", o, SW); label("x", (15, 0), E); label("y", (0, 15), N); //label("T(2, 0)", t, S + 0.6 * E); label("C(0, p)", c, W); [/asy]
solution: To find the area of ABC in terms of p, we find the area of ABOQ and subtract out the areas of ACQ and BCO. Both QA and OB are horizontal, so QA is parallel to OB. Thus, ABOQ is a trapezoid with bases AQ and OB. Since OQ is vertical, its length is the height of the trapezoid, so the area of ABOQ is 1/2· QO · (QA+OB)=1/2· 12 · (2+12)=84. Since ACQ has a right angle at Q, its area is 1/2· QA· QC=1/2· (2-0)· (12-p)=12-p. Since COB has a right angle at O, its area is 1/2· OB· CO = 1/2· (12-0)· (p-0)=6p. Thus, the area of ABC is 84-6p-(12-p)=72-5p. Then 72-5p=27 or 5p=45, so p=9.

question: Medians DP and EQ of DEF are perpendicular. If DP= 18 and EQ = 24, then what is DF?
solution: [asy] pair D,EE,F,P,Q,G; G = (0,0); D = (1.2,0); P= (-0.6,0); EE = (0,1.6); Q = (0,-0.8); F = 2*Q - D; draw(P–D–EE–F–D); draw(EE–Q); label("D",D,E); label("P",P,NW); label("Q",Q,SE); label("E",EE,N); label("F",F,SW); draw(rightanglemark(Q,G,D,3.5)); label("G",G,SW); [/asy] Point G is the centroid of DEF, so DG:GP = EG:GQ = 2:1. Therefore, DG = 2/3(DP) = 12 and QG = 1/3(EQ) =8, so applying the Pythagorean Theorem to QGD gives us QD = √(QG^2 + GD^2) = √(64+144) = √(16(4+9)) = 4√(13), which means DF = 2 QD = 8√(13).

question: Suppose ABC is a scalene right triangle, and P is the point on hypotenuse AC such that ∠ABP = 45^∘. Given that AP = 1 and CP = 2, compute the area of ABC.
solution: [asy] pair A,B,C,P; B = (0,0); A = (0,1); C = (2,0); P = A + (C-A)/3; draw(P–B–A–C–B); label("B",B,SW); label("A",A,NW); label("C",C,SE); label("P",P,NE); [/asy] Notice that BP bisects the right angle at B. Thus, the Angle Bisector Theorem tells us that AB/BC = AP/PC = 1/2. So, we have AB = x and BC = 2x for some x. By the Pythagorean theorem, we have 5x^2 =AC^2 = 9, so x^2 = 9/5. Finally, the desired area 1/2(x)(2x) = x^2 = 9/5.

question: Chuck the llama is tied to the corner of a 2 m by 3 m shed on a 3 m leash. How much area (in square meters) does Chuck have in which to play if he can go only around the outside of the shed? [asy] draw((0,0)–(15,0)–(15,10)–(0,10)–cycle,black+linewidth(1)); draw((15,10)–(27,19),black+linewidth(1)); dot((27,19)); label("Shed",(7.5,5)); label("CHUCK",(27,19),N); label("2",(0,0)–(0,10),W); label("3",(0,0)–(15,0),S); label("3",(15,10)–(27,19),SE); [/asy]
solution: When Chuck has the leash extended to its full length, he can move in a 270^∘ arc, or 3/4 of a full circle about the point where the leash is attached. (He is blocked from going further by the shed.) [asy] draw((0,0)–(15,0)–(15,10)–(0,10)–cycle,black+linewidth(1)); draw((15,10)–(27,19),black+linewidth(1)); dot((27,19)); label("Shed",(7.5,5)); label("2",(0,0)–(0,10),W); label("3",(0,0)–(15,0),S); label("3",(15,10)–(27,19),SE); draw((0,10)..(3,19)..(6,22)..(24,22)..(27,19)..(30,10)..(27,1)..(24,-2)..(15,-5),black+linewidth(1)+dashed); draw((15,0)–(15,-5),black+linewidth(1)+dashed); [/asy] The area that he can play inside this circle is 3/4 of the area of a full circle of radius 3, or 3/4×π(3^2)=27/4π. When the leash is extended fully to the left, Chuck just reaches the top left corner of the shed, so can go no further. When the leash is extended fully to the bottom, Chuck's leash extends 1 m below the length of the shed. This means that Chuck can play in more area to the left. [asy] draw((0,0)–(15,0)–(15,10)–(0,10)–cycle,black+linewidth(1)); draw((15,10)–(27,19),black+linewidth(1)); dot((27,19)); label("Shed",(7.5,5)); label("2",(0,0)–(0,10),W); label("3",(15,10)–(27,19),SE); draw((0,10)..(3,19)..(6,22)..(24,22)..(27,19)..(30,10)..(27,1)..(24,-2)..(15,-5),black+linewidth(1)+dashed); draw((15,0)–(15,-5),black+linewidth(1)+dashed); draw((15,-5)..(11.4645,-3.5355)..(10,0),black+linewidth(1)+dashed); label("1",(15,0)–(15,-5),W); label("2",(15,0)–(15,10),E); label("3",(0,10)–(15,10),N); [/asy] This area is a 90^∘ sector of a circle of radius 1, or 1/4 of this circle. So this additional area is 1/4×π (1^2)=1/4π. So the total area that Chuck has in which to play is 27/4π + 1/4π = 28/4π = 7π m^2.

question: In the figure, ABCD is a rectangle, AZ=WC=6 units, AB=12 units and the area of trapezoid ZWCD is 120 square units. What is the area of triangle BQW?
